title: Passing events safely from an ISR

spans.text: Goal: apply “Passing events safely from an ISR” to a real program or device. The key principle is: A queue moves the event to a task, which can do longer work without blocking interrupts. In a project, follow this guidance: Do not call delay, take a mutex, allocate dynamically, or perform long Serial output in an ISR.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
Prints button event handled in task after an interrupt queues the event.

An interrupt service routine (ISR) reacts to hardware events and should do only short, non-blocking work. FreeRTOS `FromISR` APIs can send a queue item or notification; move sensor reads, logging, and protocol work to a task. The correct ISR API, IRAM placement, and pin interrupt support depend on the target and board.

Key line: `void IRAM_ATTR buttonIsr() { const int event = 1; BaseType_t higherPriorityTaskWoken = pdFALSE; if (events == nullptr || xQueueSendFromISR(events, &event, &higherPriorityTaskWoken) != pdPASS) { portENTER_CRITICAL_ISR(&dropMux); ++droppedEvents; portEXIT_CRITICAL_ISR(&dropMux); } if (higherPriorityTaskWoken == pdTRUE) portYIELD_FROM_ISR(); }`
What it does: A queue moves the event to a task, which can do longer work without blocking interrupts.
Why it is used: Do not call delay, take a mutex, allocate dynamically, or perform long Serial output in an ISR.
If omitted or changed: Buttons bounce; define debounce and full-queue behavior on real hardware.
